description.en: Ce chapitre présente les concepts clés et la configuration nécessaires pour créer des workflows agentiques avec LlamaIndex. À la fin, vous aurez un agent IA pleinement opérationnel construit avec LlamaIndex, prêt à traiter des tâches concrètes.

Ce cours se réalise directement dans Neopolis avec des activités interactives. Pour les mises en situation, préparez un chatbot IA autorisé par votre organisation ; ne partagez jamais de données sensibles, de mots de passe ou de clés API.

projectorSlides.title: Qu’est-ce qu’un agent ?
projectorSlides.script: Before we dive into coding our agent, let’s answer a fundamental question: what exactly is an AI agent? And how is it different from just calling the GPT model directly?

projectorSlides.title: Limites des LLM
projectorSlides.script:
A standard GPT model is like a brilliant but single-minded expert: if we ask it a question, it gives us an answer from its training knowledge. This is already very helpful, but it doesn’t do anything beyond giving text responses.

If it doesn’t know something, it can’t go fetch information or take actions unless we explicitly feed it more data.
projectorSlides.content:
$$

- Les LLM sont puissants mais limités 

$$

- Répondent avec du texte appris à l’entraînement 

$$

- Ne récupèrent pas d’infos ni n’agissent sans nouvelles données
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
$$

- Les LLM sont puissants mais limités 

$$

- Répondent avec du texte appris à l’entraînement 

$$

- Ne récupèrent pas d’infos ni n’agissent sans nouvelles données

projectorSlides.title: Agents : vue d’ensemble
projectorSlides.script: An agent, on the other hand, is a system that leverages an AI model to interact with its environment to achieve a user-defined objective. It combines reasoning, planning, and executing actions to fulfill tasks, including tasks that need external tools to be fulfilled.
projectorSlides.content:
$$

- Exploiter un modèle d’IA pour interagir 

- Capacités : 
  - Raisonnement 
  - Planification 
  - Exécution via des outils 

$$
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
$$

- Exploiter un modèle d’IA pour interagir 

- Capacités : 
  - Raisonnement 
  - Planification 
  - Exécution via des outils

projectorSlides.title: Agents : vue d’ensemble
projectorSlides.script:
Imagine you had an AI that, when faced with a tough question, could decide whether to search the web to find the answer or to make some step-by-step calculations: that’s what an agent does.

It can plan a series of steps, use external resources, and orchestrate those steps to fulfill a task. By doing so, it can handle more complex or open‑ended tasks by breaking them down and interacting with the world as needed.

In essence, an agent has a bit of “agency” – hence the name.
projectorSlides.content:
- Scénario :
 - IA pouvant choisir recherche web ou calculs pas à pas
 - Gère des tâches complexes ou ouvertes 
 - Décompose en étapes et utilise des outils
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
- Scénario :
 - IA pouvant choisir recherche web ou calculs pas à pas
 - Gère des tâches complexes ou ouvertes 
 - Décompose en étapes et utilise des outils

projectorSlides.title: LLM vs agents
projectorSlides.script:
So when should we use a simple LLM versus an agent? If our task is straightforward and self-contained (like “summarize this text” or “translate this paragraph”), a direct LLM call is usually enough. But if the task might require fetching new information, using multiple steps, or handling conditional decisions (like “research this topic and compile a report with sources”), an agentic approach really excels.

Agents are also great when we want the AI to be extensible – for example, giving it a calculator tool for math or internet access for up‑to‑date information.
projectorSlides.content:
$$

- LLM :
	- Si la tâche est simple 

> "Résumez ce texte…" 

- Agent :
	- Si la tâche exige plusieurs étapes, infos externes ou décisions conditionnelles 
    - Ou si l’on veut ajouter un outil 

> "Faites des recherches sur ce sujet…"
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
$$

blocks.transcript:
1. Qu’est-ce qu’un agent ?
Before we dive into coding our agent, let’s answer a fundamental question: what exactly is an AI agent? And how is it different from just calling the GPT model directly?

2. Limites des LLM
A standard GPT model is like a brilliant but single-minded expert: if we ask it a question, it gives us an answer from its training knowledge. This is already very helpful, but it doesn’t do anything beyond giving text responses.

If it doesn’t know something, it can’t go fetch information or take actions unless we explicitly feed it more data.

3. Agents : vue d’ensemble
An agent, on the other hand, is a system that leverages an AI model to interact with its environment to achieve a user-defined objective. It combines reasoning, planning, and executing actions to fulfill tasks, including tasks that need external tools to be fulfilled.

4. Agents : vue d’ensemble
Imagine you had an AI that, when faced with a tough question, could decide whether to search the web to find the answer or to make some step-by-step calculations: that’s what an agent does.

It can plan a series of steps, use external resources, and orchestrate those steps to fulfill a task. By doing so, it can handle more complex or open‑ended tasks by breaking them down and interacting with the world as needed.

In essence, an agent has a bit of “agency” – hence the name.

5. LLM vs agents
So when should we use a simple LLM versus an agent? If our task is straightforward and self-contained (like “summarize this text” or “translate this paragraph”), a direct LLM call is usually enough. But if the task might require fetching new information, using multiple steps, or handling conditional decisions (like “research this topic and compile a report with sources”), an agentic approach really excels.

Agents are also great when we want the AI to be extensible – for example, giving it a calculator tool for math or internet access for up‑to‑date information.

6. Flux de travail agentiques
In this course, we’re focusing on agentic workflows – essentially, we’ll be building these more capable AI assistants. We’ll start simple, with one agent and one tool, and gradually increase complexity, up to developing a deep research agentic workflow that can perform its own research and critique it.

7. Passons à la pratique !
Exciting, right? Let’s get into it.

title.en: Les agents ont-ils de la mémoire ?
title.fr: Les agents ont-ils de la mémoire ?

projectorSlides.title: Les agents se souviennent-ils ?
projectorSlides.script: Now that we have a working agent, a question arises: do agents remember? If we run the agent twice, does it recall what happened the first time?

projectorSlides.title: Sans état vs. mémoire
projectorSlides.script: By default, most simple agents (including our AgentWorkflow so far) are stateless between runs. That means if we ask it one question now and another later, it doesn’t remember the earlier conversation or any info we gave it. Each interaction is a fresh start, as if meeting for the first time.
projectorSlides.content:
Agents :

- Sans état par défaut 
- Ne retiennent pas l’info entre sessions 
- S’exécutent indépendamment à chaque fois
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
Agents :

- Sans état par défaut 
- Ne retiennent pas l’info entre sessions 
- S’exécutent indépendamment à chaque fois

projectorSlides.title: La mémoire compte
projectorSlides.script: Human conversations, of course, are built on context: we remember what was said earlier. Similarly, more advanced AI applications often need to maintain context or memory across multiple exchanges to be truly helpful.
projectorSlides.content:
$$

- La mémoire humaine fait avancer la conversation

- Les agents ont besoin de contexte pour être utiles
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
$$

- La mémoire humaine fait avancer la conversation

- Les agents ont besoin de contexte pour être utiles

projectorSlides.title: Introduction au contexte
projectorSlides.script:
For example, if we tell an AI our name in one message, we’d like it to be remembered in later replies instead of asking again.

In LlamaIndex, the key concept to maintain memory is the agent’s state or context. “Context” is like the agent’s notepad or memory bank where it can store information to recall later.
projectorSlides.content:
$$

- Exemple : se souvenir des prénoms

- LlamaIndex utilise un objet Context
	- Stocke l’info entre exécutions
    
$$
    
> _Contexte : le bloc-notes/la banque mémoire de l’agent où il stocke des infos à rappeler plus tard._
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
$$

- Exemple : se souvenir des prénoms

- LlamaIndex utilise un objet Context
	- Stocke l’info entre exécutions
    
$$
    
> _Contexte : le bloc-notes/la banque mémoire de l’agent où il stocke des infos à rappeler plus tard._

projectorSlides.title: Du sans état au contexte activé
projectorSlides.script:
By design, AgentWorkflow doesn’t automatically persist anything between runs, which is why it’s stateless by default. In other words, agents don’t inherently remember previous conversations unless we design them to.

We’ll fix that by introducing a “context” to maintain state.

This idea is important: an intelligent workflow might involve multiple runs or continuous interaction, so being able to carry information forward (like user preferences, names, or intermediate results) is key.

Now that we have a working agent, a question arises: do agents remember? If we run the agent twice, does it recall what happened the first time?

3. La mémoire compte
Human conversations, of course, are built on context: we remember what was said earlier. Similarly, more advanced AI applications often need to maintain context or memory across multiple exchanges to be truly helpful.

4. Introduction au contexte
For example, if we tell an AI our name in one message, we’d like it to be remembered in later replies instead of asking again.

In LlamaIndex, the key concept to maintain memory is the agent’s state or context. “Context” is like the agent’s notepad or memory bank where it can store information to recall later.

5. Du sans état au contexte activé
By design, AgentWorkflow doesn’t automatically persist anything between runs, which is why it’s stateless by default. In other words, agents don’t inherently remember previous conversations unless we design them to.

We’ll fix that by introducing a “context” to maintain state.

This idea is important: an intelligent workflow might involve multiple runs or continuous interaction, so being able to carry information forward (like user preferences, names, or intermediate results) is key.

6. Passons à la pratique !
We’ll see this in action in the next section.

description.en: Pourquoi se limiter à un seul agent quand vous pouvez bâtir une équipe ? Dans ce chapitre, vous découvrirez la puissance des systèmes multi-agents, où des agents spécialisés travaillent ensemble comme une équipe de recherche, chacun avec un rôle précis. Vous construirez votre propre workflow collaboratif d’agents qui cherchent, rédigent et relisent, pour montrer comment le travail d’équipe rend votre IA plus intelligente et plus scalable.

projectorSlides.title: Qu’est-ce qu’un système multi-agent ?
projectorSlides.script: Up to now, we’ve been working with a single agent, which is already powerful.

projectorSlides.title: Au-delà d’un seul agent
projectorSlides.script:
But sometimes, dividing tasks among specialized agents can be even more effective – this is where multi-agent systems come in.

In simple terms, a multi-agent system is like a team of AI agents collaborating to achieve a goal. Each agent can have its own specialty or role, and together they can tackle complex, multifaceted tasks.
projectorSlides.content:
$$

- **Agent unique** : puissant mais limité

$$

- Des **agents spécialisés** peuvent être plus efficaces 

$$

- Collaboration en **équipe d’agents**
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
$$

- **Agent unique** : puissant mais limité

$$

- Des **agents spécialisés** peuvent être plus efficaces 

$$

- Collaboration en **équipe d’agents**

projectorSlides.title: Pourquoi plusieurs agents ?
projectorSlides.script: Why might we need many agents instead of one? Think about a project like writing an extensive research report. One approach is a single agent that tries to do everything: search for info, compile it, write the report, check its own work, and return the answer. That can work, but it can also be hard for one agent to juggle all those subtasks.
projectorSlides.content:
Exemple : 
- Rédiger un rapport de recherche 
- Un agent gère : recherche, compilation, rédaction, vérification, réponse
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
Exemple : 
- Rédiger un rapport de recherche 
- Un agent gère : recherche, compilation, rédaction, vérification, réponse

projectorSlides.title: Agents spécialisés
projectorSlides.script:
Alternatively, we could have:
A ResearchAgent that’s really good at searching for information.
A WriteAgent that excels at taking information and drafting a report.
A ReviewAgent that goes over the report and suggests improvements or corrections.
projectorSlides.content:
$$

- **Agent Recherche** : collecte l’information 

$$

- **Agent Rédaction** : rédige le rapport 

$$

- **Agent Relecture** : vérifie et améliore le contenu
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
$$

- **Agent Recherche** : collecte l’information 

$$

- **Agent Rédaction** : rédige le rapport 

$$

- **Agent Relecture** : vérifie et améliore le contenu

projectorSlides.title: Comment ils collaborent
projectorSlides.script: Each of these agents can focus on its own task. The research agent doesn’t need to worry about prose style, and the WriteAgent doesn’t need to worry about how to find data, because the research agent feeds it notes. The review agent then checks the final product for quality. This divide-and-conquer strategy mirrors how human teams often work.
projectorSlides.content:
$$

- **Agent Recherche** collecte des notes

$$

- **Agent Rédaction** rédige un brouillon à partir des notes

$$

- **Agent Relecture** peaufine le résultat final
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
$$

- **Agent Recherche** collecte des notes

$$

- **Agent Rédaction** rédige un brouillon à partir des notes

$$

- **Agent Relecture** peaufine le résultat final

projectorSlides.title: Quand monter en échelle
projectorSlides.script:
Another scenario is when tasks need to be done in parallel or require different knowledge domains. Instead of overloading one agent with everything, we spin up multiple agents. 

When should we scale from one agent to many? Usually when the task naturally breaks into parts, or when one agent alone struggles due to prompt length or complexity. If we find ourselves giving one agent a large prompt “first do this, then that, then that…”, it might be a sign to split tasks. LLMs sometimes struggle if you give them too many tools at once, so splitting our tools across multiple agents can help with that, too.
projectorSlides.content:
- Si les tâches se divisent naturellement 

- Si un agent peine avec des prompts complexes ou trop d’outils
projectorSlides.contentLeft:
- Si les tâches se divisent naturellement 

- Si un agent peine avec des prompts complexes ou trop d’outils

projectorSlides.title: AgentWorkflow intégré
projectorSlides.script:
In LlamaIndex, the AgentWorkflow is actually built to handle multiple agents internally. It allows agents to hand off tasks to each other. For example, after our ResearchAgent gathers info, it can hand off to the WriteAgent to produce the report.

The framework manages the sequence of events and passing of context between them.

However, multi-agent systems also bring complexity. We need to design how they communicate, what each knows or doesn’t know, and how they coordinate. It’s a bit like software architecture but for AI behaviors.

Multi-agent systems add a layer of complexity but also open up a new world of possibilities.

$$

- LlamaIndex `AgentWorkflow` 

$$

- Gère automatiquement la passation de tâches entre agents 

$$

- Ajoute de la complexité

$$

Up to now, we’ve been working with a single agent, which is already powerful.

2. Au-delà d’un seul agent
But sometimes, dividing tasks among specialized agents can be even more effective – this is where multi-agent systems come in.

In simple terms, a multi-agent system is like a team of AI agents collaborating to achieve a goal. Each agent can have its own specialty or role, and together they can tackle complex, multifaceted tasks.
